assumptions.text: The 'complete loss of thrust generation' failure condition is assessed as hull loss for all airborne phases on the basis that the aircraft cannot reach a suitable aerodrome from any airborne phase at or below FL260 with zero thrust, given the point-to-point mission profile to a semi-prepared strip with no diversion infrastructure.
assumptions.rationale: AEO-SDD-0001 states maximum operating altitude FL260 and the mission as point-to-point to a semi-prepared strip; no glide performance data or diversion aerodrome proximity data are provided to assess whether a dead-stick landing at an alternate is achievable.
assumptions.ifWrong: If glide performance and diversion aerodrome proximity data show a controlled forced landing is achievable, the aircraft-axis level for SF-001-TL in some phases may fall below hull loss and the severity may reduce from Catastrophic to Hazardous for those phases.

citations.quote: Maximum operating altitude FL260
The destination is a semi-prepared strip constructed for the project and not maintained to commercial standards.

assumptions.text: The 'symmetric' qualifier in SF-001-PL is interpreted as equal thrust reduction on both sides such that no net yawing moment is generated at the aircraft level; any asymmetric component is captured by SF-001-PL2.
assumptions.rationale: The SDD does not define what constitutes a 'symmetric' partial loss in terms of engine pairing or thrust level; the FCIM entry separates symmetric and asymmetric partial loss but does not define the boundary condition.
assumptions.ifWrong: If a 'symmetric' partial loss in practice generates a residual yawing moment (e.g. due to engine pairing on the same hydraulic system), the directional control demand increases and the severity may rise from Major to Hazardous.

assumptions.text: The crew is assumed to be aware of the uncommanded thrust change via the consolidated crew alert list and engine parameter displays, and to take corrective action within the time available in the applicable flight phase.
assumptions.rationale: AEO-HF-0001 states the alerting system consolidates all system status into a single prioritised crew alert list, but the aural inventory, precedence, and phase-dependent inhibit windows are TBD (open items in §8); the assumption that the crew receives timely annunciation in all phases cannot be confirmed until those items are resolved.
assumptions.ifWrong: If annunciation is inhibited or delayed in a critical phase (e.g. takeoff roll), the crew-unaware case applies and the severity of the uncommanded thrust change may rise to Hazardous or Catastrophic depending on the phase and the magnitude of the thrust change.

citations.quote: Phase-dependent inhibits during takeoff and landing: windows and inhibited set [TBD]

assumptions.text: The landing distance margin (1,800 m requirement, ~1,080 m predicted rollout) is assumed to be sufficient to arrest an uncommanded thrust increase on approach with crew action, pending quantified landing performance data.
assumptions.rationale: V-speeds, autobrake levels, and go-around performance data are all TBD per AEO-HF-0001 open items 28 and 96; without these, the time available for crew response to an uncommanded thrust increase on approach cannot be calculated.
assumptions.ifWrong: If performance analysis shows the crew cannot arrest a runway exceedance within 1,800 m following an uncommanded thrust increase on approach, the aircraft-axis level rises to 'large' and the severity of SF-001-M rises from Major to Hazardous.

citations.quote: The landing distance requirement is 1,800 m (6,000 ft) on such a surface. Predicted landing rollout at maximum landing weight is approximately 1,080 m.

assumptions.text: The hold is assumed to be unoccupied in flight for all failure conditions assessed in this turn, so the occupant-axis effects are limited to the flight crew (two to four persons).
assumptions.rationale: AEO-SDD-0001 and AEO-HF-0001 both state the hold is not occupied in flight and the aircraft carries flight crew only; this is marked [GIVEN] in AEO-HF-0001 §2.
assumptions.ifWrong: If the hold were occupied (e.g. a special condition or a deviation from the operating concept), the occupant-axis effects would need to be reassessed and severities may increase.

items.fcDesc: Complete loss of thrust generation (all four engines), all flight phases
items.effAc: Loss of all four engines removes all propulsive force. On the ground at or before V1, the aircraft can be stopped within the available distance (1,800 m requirement, ~1,080 m predicted rollout). Airborne, the aircraft cannot maintain altitude or execute a go-around; controlled flight is limited to a glide. With no thrust available, the crew cannot reach a suitable aerodrome from cruise altitude at FL260 maximum; the aircraft is lost. This constitutes hull loss across all airborne phases. The landing distance requirement of 1,800 m on a semi-prepared surface with predicted rollout of ~1,080 m means any braking degradation in a forced landing is assessed against that margin with no thrust-based go-around available.
items.effCrew: With all four engines failed airborne, the crew faces an immediate, high-workload emergency requiring simultaneous management of glide path, restart attempts, and diversion planning. The alerting system consolidates all system status into a single prioritised crew alert list with associated procedures; however, with all AC generation lost, the RAM air turbine deploys automatically supplying system C and an emergency generator. Battery-only endurance is displayed. The crew cannot be relied upon to perform all tasks accurately and completely under the time pressure of a forced landing from cruise altitude at FL260, constituting fatalities or incapacitation in the hull-loss outcome.
items.effPax: Hold is not occupied in flight; the aircraft carries flight crew only (nominal two, provision for four). In the hull-loss outcome, multiple fatalities result among the flight crew. No passenger occupants are present.
items.severityRationale: All three axes reach their top step. Hull loss is the credited outcome for all airborne phases: with all propulsive force removed and no means of reaching a suitable aerodrome from FL260, the aircraft cannot continue safe flight and landing. Per AC 25.1309-1B Note 1 to §3.1.5: 'A failure condition that would prevent continued safe flight and landing should be classified as catastrophic.' The governing definition phrase is: 'multiple fatalities, usually with the loss of the airplane,' AC 25.1309-1B §3.1.5. The crew and occupant axes follow automatically from hull loss per the joint top-step rule. On the ground at or before V1, the aircraft can be stopped; however, the worst-case phase (any airborne phase) drives the overall classification to Catastrophic. Safety objective: ≤1×10⁻⁹ per flight hour.

items.fcDesc: Partial loss of thrust generation — symmetric (reduced thrust available, all remaining engines operating, crew aware), all flight phases
items.effAc: Symmetric reduction in available thrust reduces climb gradient, reduces go-around capability, and may require a diversion or a reduced-weight landing. With four engines and symmetric loss, directional control is not compromised. The aircraft retains the ability to continue flight on the remaining thrust, but safety margins are reduced: the 1,800 m landing distance requirement on a semi-prepared surface with ~1,080 m predicted rollout leaves limited margin, and reduced thrust on approach or go-around narrows that margin further. The degree of reduction in safety margins depends on the number of engines affected and the thrust level remaining; the worst credible symmetric partial loss (e.g. two engines on opposite sides) is the sizing case for this condition. The aircraft is not lost but experiences a significant reduction in safety margins and functional capabilities.
items.effCrew: The crew receives annunciation via the consolidated crew alert list. The crew must identify the affected engines, assess remaining performance, revise the landing plan, and coordinate with ATC. The dispatch concept (two-sector decision, no line maintenance at the strip) means the crew must also assess the return sector. Workload is significantly increased but the crew can be expected to perform their tasks; the condition does not rise to excessive workload impairing task performance. This constitutes a significant increase in crew workload.
items.effPax: Hold is not occupied in flight; flight crew only. Physical distress is not expected given the aircraft remains under control, but the crew may experience physical discomfort from the workload and urgency of the diversion.
items.severityRationale: The worst axis is 'significant' on both the aircraft and crew axes, which maps to Major. The aircraft retains controlled flight but with a significant reduction in safety margins and functional capabilities, and the crew faces a significant increase in workload. The governing definition phrase is: 'significant reduction in safety margins or functional capabilities,' AC 25.1309-1B §3.1.3. The occupant axis (discomfort, flight crew only) is consistent with Major and does not drive the class higher. The condition does not reach Hazardous because the aircraft is not lost, directional control is maintained (symmetric loss), and the crew can be relied upon to perform their tasks. ASSUMPTION: 'symmetric' is interpreted as equal thrust loss on both sides such that no net yawing moment is generated; if the loss is not perfectly symmetric in practice, the asymmetric case (SF-001-PL2) applies. Safety objective: ≤1×10⁻⁵ per flight hour.

items.fcDesc: Uncommanded thrust change (one or more engines), crew aware, all flight phases
items.effAc: An uncommanded thrust change on one or more engines produces an unintended change in the aircraft's energy state and, if asymmetric, a yawing moment. The outboard engine moment arm is 28.0 m (0.35 of the 80.0 m semi-span), making an uncommanded change on an outboard engine the most demanding directional case. The flight control system is sized for an outboard engine failure at V1 with the maximum blade payload, providing rudder authority for the worst-case asymmetric thrust event. An uncommanded increase in thrust on approach or landing could cause a runway exceedance against the 1,800 m / 1,080 m margin. An uncommanded decrease is bounded by the partial-loss case. The crew is aware (annunciated via the consolidated alert list). With crew action, the aircraft can be controlled; safety margins are significantly reduced during the transient and recovery. The condition does not result in hull loss provided the crew acts.
items.effCrew: The crew must identify the affected engine(s), apply corrective control inputs, and manage the resulting energy and directional deviation. On takeoff, the identification task among four engines at the 28.0 m moment arm is a named design case (AEO-HF-0001 §7.1, B.3.2, B.16 item 32). The alerting system provides annunciation. Workload is significantly increased; in the most demanding phase (takeoff or approach), the crew must simultaneously maintain directional control and manage the thrust anomaly. The condition constitutes a significant increase in crew workload; the crew can be relied upon to perform their tasks with the available controls and annunciation, but the task is demanding.
items.effPax: Hold is not occupied in flight; flight crew only. Physical discomfort from the transient manoeuvre is possible. No injuries are expected if the crew successfully recovers the aircraft.
items.severityRationale: The worst axis is 'significant' on both the aircraft and crew axes, mapping to Major. The aircraft experiences a significant reduction in safety margins during the uncommanded thrust transient, and the crew faces a significant increase in workload to recover. The governing definition phrase is: 'significant reduction in safety margins or functional capabilities,' AC 25.1309-1B §3.1.3. The condition does not reach Hazardous because: (a) the flight control system is sized for the outboard engine failure case at V1 with maximum payload, providing sufficient rudder authority; (b) the crew is aware via annunciation; (c) hull loss is not the credited outcome with crew action. OPEN ITEM: the severity of an uncommanded thrust increase on approach against the 1,800 m / 1,080 m landing margin has not been quantified — if analysis shows the crew cannot arrest a runway exceedance in the available distance, the aircraft-axis level may rise to 'large' and the severity to Hazardous. This should be revisited when landing performance data (V-speeds, autobrake levels) are available (AEO-HF-0001 open items 28, 96). Safety objective: ≤1×10⁻⁵ per flight hour (pending resolution of the open item above).

assumptions.text: The credited outcome for SF-001-TL in all airborne phases is hull loss, on the basis that no thrust from any source is available and the 1,800 m semi-prepared strip with approximately 1,080 m predicted rollout provides insufficient margin for a powerless forced landing.
assumptions.rationale: AEO-SDD-0001 states the landing distance requirement and predicted rollout but does not explicitly characterise the outcome of a four-engine-out forced landing on the semi-prepared strip. The hull-loss credit is an engineering judgment derived from the absence of any thrust and the tight landing margin.
assumptions.ifWrong: If a powerless forced landing on the strip is survivable (e.g. due to surface characteristics or aircraft glide performance), the SF-001-TL severity could be revised downward from Catastrophic to Hazardous, which would change the safety objective from Extremely Improbable to Extremely Remote.
assumptions.usedFor: Complete loss of thrust generation (all four engines), crew aware

assumptions.text: The hold is unoccupied in flight for all failure conditions assessed in this turn; the only occupants are the flight crew (nominal two, provision for four on the flight deck).
assumptions.rationale: AEO-SDD-0001 §1.1 and AEO-HF-0001 §2 both state the hold is not occupied in flight. This assumption is load-bearing for the occupant-axis classification of every row, since it eliminates passenger fatalities as a separate axis driver.
assumptions.ifWrong: If the hold were occupied, the occupant-axis classification for SF-001-TL and SF-001-PL2 would be unchanged (multiple fatalities / serious injury respectively) but the rationale would need to account for hold occupants separately.

assumptions.text: For SF-001-PL (symmetric partial loss), the condition is assumed to remain within the dispatch case (not all engines simultaneously at reduced thrust to zero), so continued safe flight and landing is achievable and hull loss is not the credited outcome.
assumptions.rationale: AEO-SDD-0001 §5.1.3 addresses loss of any one engine but does not define the boundary between partial loss and complete loss for multiple engines simultaneously. The Major classification depends on this boundary being respected.
assumptions.ifWrong: If symmetric partial loss can degrade to a level that prevents continued safe flight and landing (e.g. all four engines at significantly reduced thrust simultaneously), the severity would rise to Hazardous or Catastrophic and the safety objective would change accordingly.

assumptions.text: For SF-001-PL2 (asymmetric partial loss), the worst-case phase is takeoff with an outboard engine failure at V1, and the rudder authority available is sufficient to maintain directional control within the dispatch case, consistent with AEO-SDD-0001 §5.3.3.
assumptions.rationale: AEO-SDD-0001 §5.3.3 states the sizing case for directional control is an outboard engine failure at V1 with the maximum blade payload, but does not confirm that all partial-loss asymmetric cases are within the rudder authority envelope. The Hazardous classification depends on this.
assumptions.ifWrong: If rudder authority is insufficient for certain asymmetric partial-loss cases (e.g. two engines on one side partially reduced), the severity could rise to Catastrophic for those sub-cases.
assumptions.usedFor: Partial loss of thrust generation — asymmetric (thrust loss concentrated on one side, crew aware)

citations.quote: The sizing case for directional control is an outboard engine failure at V1 with the maximum blade payload

assumptions.text: For SF-001-M (uncommanded thrust change), the FADEC overspeed and overtemperature protection limits the upper bound of any uncommanded thrust increase, so the condition does not escalate to hull loss within the dispatch case.
assumptions.rationale: AEO-SDD-0001 §5.1.6 states the FADEC protects against overspeed and overtemperature without crew intervention, but does not quantify the maximum uncommanded thrust excursion possible before FADEC intervention. The Hazardous (not Catastrophic) classification depends on this protection being effective.
assumptions.ifWrong: If FADEC protection is insufficient to bound the uncommanded thrust increase (e.g. a FADEC failure mode that commands maximum thrust without limit), the severity could rise to Catastrophic for the takeoff asymmetric case.
assumptions.usedFor: Uncommanded thrust change (one or more engines), crew aware

assumptions.text: For SF-001-M2 (erroneous thrust response, crew aware), the crew can detect the discrepancy between commanded and delivered thrust via the engine parameter display and compensate using the mechanically independent individual thrust levers, so continued safe flight and landing is not prevented.
assumptions.rationale: AEO-HF-0001 §6.2 and §6.3 describe engine parameter display capability but do not define the detection latency or the crew response time available in the takeoff phase. The Major classification depends on the crew being able to detect and compensate within the available time.
assumptions.ifWrong: If the crew cannot detect and compensate within the available time on takeoff (e.g. due to display latency or workload), the severity could rise to Hazardous for the takeoff phase, changing the safety objective.
assumptions.usedFor: Erroneous thrust response to crew command (thrust delivered differs from commanded value), crew aware

assumptions.rationale: AEO-HF-0001 §B.16 item 32 explicitly names engine identification among four as an unresolved design case. The crew-axis classifications for SF-001-PL2 and SF-001-M depend on the crew being able to identify the affected engine within the available time.

items.fcDesc: Complete loss of thrust generation (all four engines), crew aware
items.effAc: All four engines inoperative. On the ground or at low speed during takeoff roll, the aircraft can be stopped within the available distance if below V1; above V1 or airborne, no thrust is available from any source and continued flight is not possible. The aircraft cannot maintain altitude, execute a go-around, or reach a suitable aerodrome. Hull loss is the expected outcome in all airborne phases. The landing distance requirement of 1,800 m on a semi-prepared surface with predicted rollout of approximately 1,080 m leaves no margin for a powerless forced landing. Accumulator braking (six applications) and free-fall gear extension remain available but cannot compensate for the absence of thrust on approach. Outcome: loss of the aircraft in all airborne phases.
items.effCrew: With hull loss as the credited outcome, crew fatalities or incapacitation result. No further crew-workload evidence is required or applicable once the aircraft is lost.
items.effPax: Hold is unoccupied in flight; flight crew only (nominal two, provision for four on the flight deck). Hull loss results in multiple fatalities among the flight-deck occupants.
items.severityRationale: All four engines inoperative in any airborne phase prevents continued safe flight and landing. Per AC 25.1309-1B §3.1.5 Note 1: 'A failure condition that would prevent continued safe flight and landing should be classified as catastrophic.' The governing definition phrase is 'multiple fatalities, usually with the loss of the airplane' (AC 25.1309-1B §3.1.5). All three axes reach their top step jointly: hull loss on the aircraft axis carries crew fatalities or incapacitation and multiple fatalities on the occupant axis automatically.

items.fcDesc: Partial loss of thrust generation — symmetric (reduced thrust available on one or more engines, symmetrically distributed, crew aware)
items.effAc: Thrust is reduced but not eliminated, and the reduction is symmetric so no net yawing moment is introduced. On takeoff, reduced thrust may require a longer ground roll or reduce climb gradient below obstacle-clearance requirements, depending on the degree of reduction and the number of engines affected. In cruise, the aircraft may be unable to maintain altitude or speed at the planned flight level, requiring drift-down; with a maximum operating altitude of FL260 and a 600–2,000 nm sector, diversion options exist. On approach and landing, reduced go-around thrust degrades the ability to execute a missed approach. The 1,800 m landing distance requirement on a semi-prepared surface is not directly affected by symmetric thrust reduction once on the ground. Remaining thrust from unaffected engines or from partial thrust on affected engines provides continued flight capability; the condition does not by itself prevent continued safe flight and landing. Significant reduction in safety margins and functional capabilities is the aircraft-axis finding.
items.effCrew: Crew is aware. The alerting system consolidates engine parameter data to the crew alert list with associated procedures. The crew must identify the affected engine(s), assess the degree of reduction, and manage the flight path and fuel accordingly. On takeoff this task is time-critical; in cruise it is manageable within normal workload. The four-engine identification task (which of four has reduced thrust, at what point in the takeoff) is a named design case per AEO-HF-0001 §B.3.2 and §B.16 item 32; the crew's means of identification is not fully defined. Significant increase in crew workload is the crew-axis finding, consistent with Major.
items.effPax: Hold is unoccupied in flight. Flight-deck occupants (two to four) experience no direct physical distress from a symmetric partial thrust loss that does not result in hull loss. Physical discomfort is not expected from the flight-path effects of a symmetric reduction alone.
items.severityRationale: Symmetric partial thrust loss reduces climb gradient, go-around capability, and cruise performance without preventing continued safe flight and landing. The governing definition phrase is 'significant reduction in safety margins or functional capabilities' (AC 25.1309-1B §3.1.3, Major). Crew workload is significantly increased, particularly on takeoff where engine identification among four is a named open design case (AEO-HF-0001 §B.16 item 32), consistent with 'significant increase in flightcrew workload' (AC 25.1309-1B §3.1.3). The occupant axis does not drive the class. Worst axis: Major.

items.fcDesc: Partial loss of thrust generation — asymmetric (thrust loss concentrated on one side, crew aware)
items.effAc: Thrust loss on one side introduces a net yawing moment. The outboard engine moment arm is 28.0 m (0.35 of the 80.0 m semi-span); loss of an outboard engine produces the largest yawing moment and is the sizing case for directional control. The rudder authority requirement is set by this case per AEO-SDD-0001 §5.3.3. On takeoff at or above V1 the aircraft is designed to continue; below V1 the takeoff is rejected. In cruise and approach, asymmetric thrust requires rudder and aileron to maintain heading and wings level, reducing available control authority for other tasks. If the asymmetry is severe (e.g. two engines on one side lost — outside the dispatch case per §5.1.3), directional control may not be maintainable. Within the dispatch case (one engine), continued safe flight and landing is achievable but with a large reduction in safety margins and functional capabilities, particularly on the semi-prepared strip with its 1,800 m / 1,080 m margin.
items.effCrew: Crew is aware. Directional control demands immediate and sustained rudder input; on takeoff this is time-critical and the identification of which of four engines has failed is a named design case (AEO-HF-0001 §B.16 item 32). Physical distress or excessive workload is possible during the takeoff phase, particularly with an outboard engine failure at V1 on a semi-prepared surface. In cruise the workload is elevated but manageable. The crew cannot be fully relied upon to perform all tasks accurately during the takeoff phase with an outboard asymmetric failure, consistent with Hazardous on the crew axis for the worst phase.
items.effPax: Hold is unoccupied in flight. Flight-deck occupants may experience physical distress during the directional-control recovery on takeoff. If directional control is lost, hull loss and multiple fatalities result; within the dispatch case, serious injury is possible but not the expected outcome.
items.severityRationale: Asymmetric partial thrust loss, worst case an outboard engine at V1, produces the largest yawing moment the directional control system is sized against. Within the dispatch case the aircraft can continue, but with a large reduction in safety margins and functional capabilities and physical distress or excessive workload on the crew during the takeoff phase. The governing definition phrase is 'large reduction in safety margins or functional capabilities' and 'physical distress or excessive workload such that the flightcrew cannot be relied upon to perform their tasks accurately or completely' (AC 25.1309-1B §3.1.4, Hazardous). The occupant axis (serious or fatal injury to a small number) is consistent with Hazardous and does not independently drive the class above it. Worst axis: Hazardous.

items.fcDesc: Uncommanded thrust change (one or more engines), crew aware
items.effAc: One or more engines produce thrust that differs from the commanded value without crew input. If the uncommanded change is symmetric (all engines equally affected), the primary effect is a speed or altitude excursion; the crew can respond by adjusting the thrust levers. If the uncommanded change is asymmetric (one or more engines on one side), a yawing moment is introduced; the magnitude depends on which engine and the degree of change. On takeoff, an uncommanded thrust increase on one side at rotation is the most critical case, potentially exceeding rudder authority if large enough. On approach, an uncommanded thrust reduction may cause undershoot. The FADEC protects against overspeed and overtemperature without crew intervention per AEO-SDD-0001 §5.1.6, limiting the upper bound of uncommanded increase. The condition does not by itself prevent continued safe flight and landing if detected and responded to promptly; however, on takeoff the time available for response is short. Large reduction in safety margins is the aircraft-axis finding for the worst phase (takeoff, asymmetric uncommanded increase).
items.effCrew: Crew is aware (annunciated via engine parameter display and alerting system). The crew must detect the uncommanded change, identify the affected engine(s), and respond. On takeoff this is time-critical; the four-engine identification task is a named design case (AEO-HF-0001 §B.16 item 32). Autothrottle engagement/disengage on the levers per AEO-HF-0001 §7.1 may complicate the response if the autothrottle is the source of the uncommanded change. Physical distress or excessive workload is possible on takeoff; in cruise the workload is significantly elevated but manageable. Crew-axis finding: large (Hazardous) for the takeoff phase worst case.
items.effPax: Hold is unoccupied in flight. Flight-deck occupants may experience physical distress during a large uncommanded thrust change on takeoff. Serious injury is possible if the excursion is not arrested; multiple fatalities are not the expected outcome within the dispatch case.
items.severityRationale: Uncommanded thrust change, worst case an asymmetric uncommanded increase on an outboard engine at takeoff, produces a yawing moment and speed excursion that demands immediate crew response under high time pressure. The governing definition phrase is 'large reduction in safety margins or functional capabilities' and 'physical distress or excessive workload such that the flightcrew cannot be relied upon to perform their tasks accurately or completely' (AC 25.1309-1B §3.1.4, Hazardous). The FADEC overspeed/overtemperature protection per AEO-SDD-0001 §5.1.6 limits the upper bound of uncommanded increase but does not eliminate the hazard. Worst axis: Hazardous. Note: if the uncommanded change is symmetric and small, the condition may be Major; the worst phase (takeoff, asymmetric) drives the classification.

items.fcDesc: Erroneous thrust response to crew command (thrust delivered differs from commanded value), crew aware
items.effAc: The engine delivers thrust that differs from what the crew commanded, but the crew is aware (engine parameter display and alerting system provide feedback). The crew can observe the discrepancy and compensate by adjusting the thrust lever position. If the erroneous response is symmetric, the primary effect is a speed or altitude excursion correctable by the crew. If asymmetric, a yawing moment is introduced. On takeoff, the time available for detection and correction is short; on approach, an erroneous thrust reduction may cause undershoot. The FADEC dual-channel architecture per AEO-SDD-0001 §5.1.2 provides protection against single-channel FADEC failures. The condition does not prevent continued safe flight and landing if the crew can compensate, but significantly reduces safety margins in critical phases. Significant reduction in safety margins and functional capabilities is the aircraft-axis finding.
items.effCrew: Crew is aware. The crew must detect the discrepancy between commanded and delivered thrust, identify the affected engine, and compensate. On takeoff this is time-critical. The four thrust levers are mechanically independent per AEO-HF-0001 §7.1, so the crew can adjust individual levers. Significant increase in crew workload is the crew-axis finding; physical distress is possible on takeoff but not the expected outcome in cruise.
items.effPax: Hold is unoccupied in flight. Flight-deck occupants experience no direct physical distress from a correctable erroneous thrust response. Physical discomfort is possible during the correction manoeuvre.
items.severityRationale: Erroneous thrust response with crew awareness allows crew compensation via individual thrust lever adjustment; continued safe flight and landing is not prevented. The governing definition phrase is 'significant reduction in safety margins or functional capabilities' (AC 25.1309-1B §3.1.3, Major). Crew workload is significantly increased, particularly on takeoff. The occupant axis does not drive the class. Worst axis: Major. Note: if the erroneous response is large and asymmetric on takeoff, the condition may approach Hazardous; the engineer should confirm whether this sub-case warrants a separate row or an upward revision.

items.fcDesc: Complete loss of thrust generation (all four engines), crew aware
items.effAc: Loss of all propulsive thrust from all four engines leaves the aircraft unable to maintain altitude or execute a go-around; the aircraft must glide to a landing. At takeoff or on approach to a semi-prepared strip with a 1,800 m requirement and no alternate propulsion, continued safe flight and landing cannot be assured. Hull loss is the credible outcome in all phases where altitude and energy are insufficient for a successful forced landing.
items.effCrew: Fatalities or incapacitation — crew are aboard the aircraft and hull loss is credited as not recoverable by crew action across the applicable phases.
items.effPax: Multiple fatalities — crew (two to four persons on the flight deck) are the only occupants; hull loss results in multiple fatalities.
items.severityRationale: Complete loss of all four engines removes all propulsive capability; the aircraft cannot maintain altitude or execute a go-around from any phase. AC 25.1309-1B Note 1 states 'A failure condition that would prevent continued safe flight and landing should be classified as catastrophic.' The governing definition phrase is: "multiple fatalities, usually with the loss of the airplane", AC 25.1309-1B §3.1.5. Hull loss drives all three axes to their top step jointly.

items.fcDesc: Partial loss of thrust generation — symmetric (reduced thrust available on one or more engines, symmetrically distributed, crew aware)
items.effAc: Symmetric reduction in available thrust degrades climb performance, reduces obstacle clearance margins, and may prevent attainment of cruise altitude or require drift-down. On takeoff, reduced thrust reduces accelerate-stop and climb-out margins. On approach and landing to a 1,800 m semi-prepared strip, a go-around may not be achievable at reduced thrust settings. Safety margins are significantly reduced but the aircraft retains directional control and the remaining engines continue to provide thrust; hull loss is not the immediate outcome with crew awareness and appropriate response.
items.effCrew: Significant increase in crew workload: the crew must identify the affected engine(s), assess thrust available, recompute performance, and manage the approach and landing against a reduced go-around capability. The alerting system consolidates engine parameter data to the crew alert list; the crew is aware. Workload is significant but within trained crew capability for a symmetric degradation.
items.effPax: No occupants other than flight crew; flight crew may experience physical discomfort associated with a non-normal approach and landing but injuries are not the expected outcome of a symmetric partial thrust loss with crew awareness.
items.severityRationale: Symmetric partial thrust loss significantly reduces climb and go-around capability and increases crew workload, but directional control is retained and the aircraft can continue to a landing. The governing definition phrase is: "significant reduction in safety margins or functional capabilities", AC 25.1309-1B §3.1.3. The aircraft axis drives the class; crew and occupant axes are consistent with Major.

items.fcDesc: Uncommanded thrust change (one or more engines), crew aware
items.effAc: An uncommanded thrust change on one or more engines produces an unintended acceleration or deceleration. If the affected engine(s) are outboard, the 28 m moment arm generates a significant yawing moment that the crew must counter with rudder; the outboard engine failure at V1 is the sizing case for directional control per the SDD. On takeoff this may result in a runway excursion or loss of directional control if the uncommanded change is large and rapid. On approach, an uncommanded thrust increase or decrease may cause a go-around or a hard landing. Safety margins are significantly to largely reduced depending on phase and magnitude; the aircraft retains control surfaces and the remaining engines, but the condition imposes an immediate and demanding control task. A large reduction in safety margins is credible for an outboard engine uncommanded change at a critical phase.
items.effCrew: Physical distress or excessive workload: an uncommanded thrust change, particularly from an outboard engine at the 28 m moment arm, imposes an immediate directional control demand. AEO-HF-0001 §7.1 records that asymmetric identification is a takeoff design case and that the geometry makes an outboard and inboard failure different problems. The crew is aware (annunciated via engine parameter display and alerting system) but the response time available at takeoff may be very short. In the worst phase (takeoff, outboard engine), workload may reach the level at which the crew cannot be relied upon to perform their tasks accurately or completely.
items.effPax: Flight crew only aboard; serious injury is possible in a runway excursion or hard landing resulting from an uncommanded thrust change at a critical phase.
items.severityRationale: An uncommanded thrust change from an outboard engine at the 28 m moment arm at a critical phase (takeoff, approach) produces a large reduction in safety margins and may impose excessive workload on the crew. The governing definition phrase is: "large reduction in safety margins or functional capabilities", AC 25.1309-1B §3.1.4, and "physical distress or excessive workload such that the flightcrew cannot be relied upon to perform their tasks accurately or completely", AC 25.1309-1B §3.1.4. The outboard moment arm geometry and the semi-prepared strip landing margin are the intensifying factors per AC 25.1309-1B §6.3.3.2. The condition does not meet Catastrophic because the aircraft retains three engines and full control surfaces, and the crew is aware; however the worst-phase effect (outboard engine at V1) drives the classification to Hazardous rather than Major.

assumptions.ifWrong: If any occupant were carried in the hold, the occupant axis on each row would need re-evaluation and could raise severity.

citations.quote: The hold is not occupied in flight. The aircraft carries flight crew only

assumptions.text: A spurious engine/APU fire warning, if actioned by the crew, results at worst in one unnecessary engine shutdown recoverable on the remaining three engines.
assumptions.rationale: The Major classification of SF-021-M rests on the aircraft continuing on remaining engines after any crew shutdown; the SDD supports one-engine-inoperative continuation but not the specific spurious-warning response.
assumptions.ifWrong: If the spurious warning could drive shutdown of more than one engine or an inboard/hydraulic-critical engine, the aircraft effect and severity of SF-021-M would increase.

citations.quote: designed to continue to a suitable aerodrome following the loss of any one engine at or after V1

assumptions.text: For SF-022 detection failure conditions, the severity-driving outcome is the consequence of an undetected/uncovered hold smoke or overheat event, not the loss of the indication in isolation.
assumptions.rationale: The provided material states detection exists with no suppression and no in-flight hold access, but does not characterise the aircraft-level outcome of a hold event, forcing me to abstain on severity rather than classify.
assumptions.ifWrong: If the detection-loss condition were classifiable on its own terms (e.g. as a monitoring-loss Minor/Major per §5.4.2), the empty severities on SF-022-TL, SF-022-PL and SF-022-PL2 would be replaced with committed classes.

citations.quote: The hold has smoke detection at nine stations along its length and no suppression

assumptions.text: The crew response to a genuine hold smoke/overheat indication is land-as-soon-as-possible to the nearest suitable aerodrome, so a spurious warning drives a precautionary diversion.
assumptions.rationale: The HF procedures document states this response for a hold smoke indication; the erroneous-warning severity leans on the crew acting on the spurious warning as if genuine.
assumptions.ifWrong: If the crew can readily discount a spurious hold warning without a diversion, SF-022-M could drop to No Safety Effect; if the diversion is more consequential, it could rise.

citations.quote: Land as soon as possible; the nearest suitable aerodrome, not the destination.

assumptions.text: The hold is unoccupied in flight, so ice-protection failure conditions have no occupant effect beyond the two-to-four flight crew.
assumptions.rationale: The occupant axis needs to know whether anyone besides flight crew is aboard; the documents state the hold is unoccupied in flight.
assumptions.ifWrong: If occupants were carried, the effPax axis and potentially the class of any hazardous outcome would change.

citations.quote: The hold is not occupied in flight. The aircraft carries flight crew only

assumptions.text: Manual selection of ice protection is available at any time independent of either ice detector, so detection failures do not remove the protection capability itself.
assumptions.rationale: Whether detection loss also disables protection determines whether the Minor/abstain call on SF-023-M/PL2 is correct; the documents state manual selection is independent.
assumptions.ifWrong: If manual protection depended on the detectors, SF-023-PL2 and SF-023-PL3 would carry a larger reduction in capability and a higher proposed class.

citations.quote: The manual selection is available at any time and does not depend on either detector

items.fcDesc: Complete loss of thrust generation
items.effAc: No thrust available from any of the four engines; the aircraft can no longer sustain flight and hull loss follows in every phase, normally with loss of the airplane.
items.effCrew: Loss of the airplane is not recoverable by crew action; fatalities or incapacitation.
items.effPax: Hold unoccupied in flight; crew aboard sustain multiple fatalities.
items.severityRationale: Total loss of propulsion in flight is not survivable and results in loss of the airplane — "multiple fatalities, usually with the loss of the airplane" (AC 25.1309-1B §3.1.5). Top-step aircraft axis carries crew and occupant axes to their top steps jointly.

source.quote: Four podded turbofans on pylons beneath the high wing provide thrust for all phases of flight

items.fcDesc: Partial loss of thrust generation — symmetric
items.effAc: Reduced total thrust available with balanced loss across the four engines; climb gradient and performance margins reduced but thrust remains distributed symmetrically with no directional asymmetry.
items.severityRationale: The SDD gives the one-engine-out continuation case and the outboard-asymmetry sizing case, but does not quantify remaining climb/performance margin for a symmetric partial thrust loss, and the number of further failures to a catastrophic outcome cannot be counted from the provided material. Aircraft-effect level (slight/significant/large) cannot be grounded, so severity is left for engineering assessment.

source.quote: The aircraft is designed to continue to a suitable aerodrome following the loss of any one engine

items.fcDesc: Uncommanded thrust change
items.effAc: Thrust on one or more engines changes without crew command; if the change is asymmetric it introduces a yawing moment about the 28.0 m outboard moment arm and a large reduction in directional-control and speed margins the crew must counter.
items.effCrew: Crew becomes aware through thrust indication and aircraft response and must identify and counter the excursion; physical distress or excessive workload where the change is asymmetric at low speed.
items.effPax: Hold unoccupied in flight; crew only aboard.
items.severityRationale: An uncommanded asymmetric thrust change at the outboard moment arm produces "a large reduction in safety margins or functional capabilities" (AC 25.1309-1B §3.1.4); remaining rudder authority is sized for the outboard-asymmetry case so continued safe flight is retained, preventing a catastrophic outcome.

source.quote: Asymmetric thrust from an outboard engine at the 28 m moment arm is the sizing case for directional control

items.fcDesc: Partial loss of thrust generation — asymmetric
items.effAc: Thrust loss concentrated on one side (single-engine loss at or after V1) yields an asymmetric thrust condition about the outboard moment arm; directional control is retained on the sizing rudder authority and the aircraft can continue to a suitable aerodrome, a large reduction in functional capability.
items.effCrew: Crew identifies and secures the affected engine and flies the engine-out profile; excessive workload at the sizing case such that the flightcrew cannot be relied upon to perform tasks with margin, though the case is a designed continuation.
items.effPax: Hold unoccupied in flight; crew only aboard.
items.severityRationale: Asymmetric partial thrust loss at the outboard moment arm is a "large reduction in safety margins or functional capabilities" (AC 25.1309-1B §3.1.4); the design continues to a suitable aerodrome after loss of one engine, so remaining capability prevents a catastrophic outcome per §6.3.3.3.

source.quote: Asymmetric thrust from an outboard engine at the 28 m moment arm is the sizing case for directional control

items.fcDesc: Erroneous thrust response to command
items.effAc: Thrust delivered differs from that commanded (more, less, or on the wrong engine); the mismatch may be symmetric or asymmetric, and an asymmetric error about the 28.0 m moment arm reduces directional-control and speed margins the crew must counter.
items.severityRationale: The provided material does not bound the magnitude or symmetry of the thrust error against command (the FADEC overspeed/overtemperature protections are stated but the error envelope for a commanded-vs-delivered mismatch is not), so the aircraft-effect level cannot be grounded and severity is left for engineering assessment. Splitting crew-aware vs crew-unaware variants also requires detection coverage not stated.

source.quote: the FADEC protects against overspeed and overtemperature without crew intervention

items.fcDesc: Complete loss of reverse thrust
items.effAc: Rollout is flown on wheel braking and spoilers alone against the 1,800 m landing distance requirement with approximately 1,080 m predicted rollout at maximum landing weight; a slight reduction in functional capabilities on a normal-condition landing where the braking margin absorbs the loss.
items.effCrew: Slight increase in flightcrew workload — the crew flies the rollout on braking against the stated margin, a task within capability on a normal surface.
items.effPax: Hold unoccupied in flight; flight crew only. No effect on occupants beyond the crew task above.
items.severityRationale: Reverse is available on the two inboard engines only; rollout on braking alone is assessed against the 1,800 m / 1,080 m margin the design rests on. Effects support Minor - "a slight reduction in safety margins or functional capabilities", AC 25.1309-1B §3.1.2. NOTE: severity hinges on the margin absorbing the loss under the surface conditions actually credited; on a degraded semi-prepared surface with reduced braking this could intensify — engineer to confirm against the landing-performance case.

source.quote: predicted landing rollout is approximately 1,080 m

items.fcDesc: Partial loss of reverse thrust
items.effAc: Reverse thrust available from one inboard engine only; rollout is flown on braking, spoilers and the remaining reverser against the 1,800 m / 1,080 m margin — a slight reduction in functional capabilities on a normal-condition landing, less severe than complete loss.
items.effCrew: Slight increase in flightcrew workload — asymmetric single-reverser thrust adds a directional element to the braking task.
items.effPax: Hold unoccupied in flight; flight crew only. No effect on occupants beyond the crew task above.
items.severityRationale: With reverse fitted to only two inboard engines, partial loss leaves one reverser plus braking against the design margin. Effects support Minor - "a slight reduction in safety margins or functional capabilities", AC 25.1309-1B §3.1.2. Directional handling with a single inboard reverser on a semi-prepared surface is [TBD] in the source and the engineer should confirm it does not intensify.

source.quote: Reverse is available on the two inboard engines only

items.fcDesc: Inadvertent reverse thrust in flight
items.effAc: Uncommanded reverse thrust from an inboard engine in flight produces a large reduction in functional capabilities up to loss of control; the design provides two independent inhibits (weight-on-wheels and radio-altimeter agreement) plus a mechanical translating-sleeve lock specifically against this, and hull loss is credited as the worst outcome where those barriers are defeated.
items.effCrew: Fatalities or incapacitation — joint with hull loss.
items.effPax: Multiple fatalities — joint with hull loss; crew are the only occupants.
items.severityRationale: Significant thrust in the direction opposite to that commanded in flight is a Part 33 hazardous engine effect and, uncontained at aircraft level, prevents continued safe flight. Effects support Catastrophic - "multiple fatalities, usually with the loss of the airplane", AC 25.1309-1B §3.1.5. The class is against the outcome when the two inhibits and the mechanical lock are all defeated; the probability of reaching this state is owned by the deterministic engine given that barrier architecture.

source.quote: Reverser deployment is inhibited in flight by weight-on-wheels and radio-altimeter agreement, with a mechanical lock

items.fcDesc: Asymmetric reverse thrust deployment
items.effPax: Hold unoccupied in flight; flight crew only.
items.severityRationale: On landing (weight-on-wheels), asymmetric single-inboard-reverser thrust produces a directional upset whose magnitude — and whether it exceeds available rudder/steering authority at the deployment speed on a semi-prepared surface — is not quantified in the provided material (two-engine reverse directional behaviour is [TBD] in AEO-HF-0001 §A.8.3). Cannot ground the aircraft or crew effect level without that handling case; severity left empty per the abstention rule. In-flight deployment is precluded by the inhibits and is covered by SF-002-M.

source.quote: directional and deceleration behaviour with two-engine reverse on a semi-prepared surface is [TBD]

items.fcDesc: Complete loss of pitch control
items.effAc: Complete loss of the ability to control the aircraft in pitch by any means; the elevators are driven from hydraulic systems A and C and a mechanical reversion path reaches stabiliser trim only, so total loss of pitch control leaves no means to arrest the flight path and results in loss of the airplane.
items.effCrew: Fatalities or incapacitation — joint with hull loss.
items.effPax: Multiple fatalities — joint with hull loss; crew are the only occupants.
items.severityRationale: Complete loss of pitch control prevents continued safe flight and landing. Effects support Catastrophic - "multiple fatalities, usually with the loss of the airplane", AC 25.1309-1B §3.1.5. Elevators are supplied from systems A and C with a mechanical stabiliser-trim reversion path; complete loss requires exhaustion of all those means, and its probability is owned by the deterministic engine.

source.quote: the elevators from A and C

items.fcDesc: Partial loss of pitch control authority
items.effAc: Pitch remains controllable but at reduced authority; every primary surface is driven by at least two actuators on different hydraulic systems and the elevators are supplied from HYD A and C, so a partial reduction leaves pitch driven. The magnitude of the residual authority against the flight envelope — and whether it is sufficient at forward centre-of-gravity with a full-length 72.6 t item — is not stated.
items.severityRationale: Cannot classify: the SDD establishes dual-actuator, dual-hydraulic pitch drive (§5.3.2) but states no residual pitch authority, handling qualities or limitations for a partial loss, and flags gains/limits scheduling on payload configuration as [TBD] (AEO-HF-0001 item 18). Without the amount of impairment against the envelope the reduction in safety margin cannot be graded.

source.quote: Every primary surface is driven by at least two actuators supplied from different hydraulic systems

items.fcDesc: Erroneous pitch response to crew command
items.effAc: The stabiliser/elevator responds to a pitch command differently from that commanded; an erroneous nose-up or nose-down response uncommanded by the crew's actual demand produces a flight-path departure the crew must arrest. Pitch is the primary flight-path axis; an erroneous response low and slow (takeoff, approach, landing) can produce a large reduction in safety margins from which recovery is not assured, consistent with loss of the airplane.
items.effCrew: Multiple fatalities usually with the loss of the airplane; the flightcrew are aboard and the hull-loss outcome is credited as not recoverable in the adverse phase.
items.effPax: No passengers are carried; the hold is unoccupied in flight, so this axis is the flight crew (fatalities or incapacitation).
items.severityRationale: "A failure condition that would result in multiple fatalities, usually with the loss of the airplane", AC 25.1309-1B §3.1.5. An erroneous pitch response in an adverse phase departs the flight path in the primary control axis; consistent with the existing SF-003-M classification in the model.

source.quote: positions the primary and secondary aerodynamic surfaces in response to pilot and autopilot commands

items.fcDesc: Uncommanded pitch motion
items.effAc: The stabiliser or elevator moves without a crew or autopilot command, producing an uncommanded pitch excursion. In the normal control law envelope protection is active, but an uncommanded excursion in an adverse phase (takeoff, approach, landing) departs the flight path in the primary axis and can produce a large reduction in safety margins from which recovery is not assured, consistent with loss of the airplane.
items.effCrew: Multiple fatalities usually with the loss of the airplane; the flightcrew are aboard and hull loss is credited as not recoverable in the adverse phase.
items.effPax: No passengers are carried; the hold is unoccupied in flight, so this axis is the flight crew (fatalities or incapacitation).
items.severityRationale: "A failure condition that would result in multiple fatalities, usually with the loss of the airplane", AC 25.1309-1B §3.1.5. Uncommanded motion in the primary pitch axis; consistent with the existing SF-003-M2 classification in the model. Envelope protection is a normal-law function and cannot be credited to alleviate below the design integrity requirement (AC 25.1309-1B §6.3.3.2).

source.quote: envelope protection active in the normal control law

items.fcDesc: Undetected pitch control authority reduction
items.effAc: Pitch authority is reduced but the reduction is not annunciated, so the crew continue their duties normally and take no action; the shortfall is discovered only when the demanded pitch cannot be achieved, characteristically low and slow. The residual authority and the point at which it becomes insufficient are not stated.
items.severityRationale: Cannot classify: this is the crew-unaware variant of the partial loss and its severity turns on how much authority remains undetected and whether loss of the annunciation itself governs. Degraded laws are annunciated (§5.3.6) but no detection coverage for a gradual authority reduction is stated, and residual pitch authority is not given. Per AC 25.1309-1B §5.4.2 loss of annunciation is itself a failure condition classified major unless shown otherwise — needs the un-annunciated effect substantiated before a class can be committed.

source.quote: Degraded laws are annunciated

items.fcDesc: Uncommanded pitch trim runaway — undetected
items.effAc: The trimmable horizontal stabiliser runs uncommanded and the runaway is not detected, so the crew take no action against it; the mistrim builds until it opposes or overpowers elevator authority. The stabiliser is all-moving and the mechanical reversion path reaches the stabiliser trim, but the trim runaway rate, the available stop or cut-out authority, and the elevator margin against a full mistrim are not stated.
items.severityRationale: Cannot classify: a stabiliser mistrim can overpower elevator authority, but the SDD gives no trim runaway rate, no runaway detection or cut-out, and no elevator margin against full mistrim, and identifies no pitch-trim protection. Whether an undetected runaway remains recoverable is exactly what is unstated, so severity is left empty rather than assumed.

source.quote: pitch by an all-moving trimmable horizontal stabiliser with elevators

items.fcDesc: Complete loss of roll control
items.effAc: Roll is by two-segment ailerons and multi-function spoilers, each surface on two hydraulic systems (ailerons B and C); with roll control wholly lost the aircraft cannot be controlled about the roll axis by any means and continued safe flight and landing is not possible — normally with hull loss.
items.effCrew: Crew cannot arrest a lateral upset; multiple fatalities and crew incapacitation follow the loss of the aircraft.
items.effPax: No occupants other than flight crew are carried in flight; the hold is unoccupied. Fatalities of the flight crew follow the loss of the aircraft.
items.severityRationale: Complete loss of a primary control axis prevents continued safe flight and landing — "A failure condition that would result in multiple fatalities, usually with the loss of the airplane", AC 25.1309-1B §3.1.5; Note 1 classifies loss of continued safe flight and landing as catastrophic.

source.quote: Roll is by two-segment ailerons and multi-function spoilers

items.fcDesc: Partial loss of roll control authority
items.effAc: Roll authority is reduced (for example loss of one hydraulic supply to the ailerons, or a spoiler group inoperative) with roll control still available. The magnitude of the reduction and the residual manoeuvre capability against the roll axis are not stated in the provided material.
items.severityRationale: Cannot classify: the SDD states ailerons are driven from two hydraulic systems and roll is by ailerons plus spoilers, but gives no roll authority margin, handling-quality data, or residual-capability figure to establish how much capability is lost; the control-law degradation levels are [TBD] in AEO-HF-0001 §B.7.1. Without the reduction magnitude the effect that would drive the class is unstated.

source.quote: the ailerons from B and C

items.fcDesc: Erroneous roll response to crew command
items.effAc: The roll response delivered differs from that commanded (wrong direction or wrong magnitude). An erroneous response on a primary control axis at low altitude — takeoff, approach or landing — produces a lateral excursion the crew cannot reliably correct and results in loss of the aircraft.
items.effCrew: Crew commands do not produce the intended roll; the mismatch drives the aircraft to an unrecoverable attitude at low height. Crew fatalities and incapacitation follow the loss of the aircraft.
items.effPax: No occupants other than flight crew are carried in flight. Fatalities of the flight crew follow the loss of the aircraft.
items.severityRationale: An erroneous primary-axis roll response at low altitude prevents continued safe flight and landing — "A failure condition that would result in multiple fatalities, usually with the loss of the airplane", AC 25.1309-1B §3.1.5; worst applicable phase (takeoff/approach/landing) drives the classification.

source.quote: three dissimilar flight control computers voting on command

items.fcDesc: Uncommanded roll motion
items.effAc: An uncommanded roll input drives the aircraft about the roll axis with no crew command. At low altitude the resulting bank develops faster than the crew can arrest it and results in loss of the aircraft.
items.effCrew: Crew must recognise and oppose an uncommanded roll while flying the aircraft; at low height the excursion is unrecoverable. Crew fatalities and incapacitation follow the loss of the aircraft.
items.effPax: No occupants other than flight crew are carried in flight. Fatalities of the flight crew follow the loss of the aircraft.
items.severityRationale: An uncommanded roll on a primary control axis at low altitude prevents continued safe flight and landing — "A failure condition that would result in multiple fatalities, usually with the loss of the airplane", AC 25.1309-1B §3.1.5; worst applicable phase drives the class.

source.quote: Roll is by two-segment ailerons and multi-function spoilers

items.fcDesc: Undetected roll control authority reduction
items.effAc: Roll control authority is reduced and the crew is not made aware of it; they continue normally and take no action, discovering the reduction only when a manoeuvre demands the missing authority. The residual authority and the manoeuvre point at which the shortfall bites are not stated in the provided material.
items.severityRationale: Cannot classify: this is the crew-unaware variant of SF-004-PL, and per AC 25.1309-1B §5.4.2 the un-annunciated case is assessed with no crew alleviation. But the same gap applies — the SDD gives no roll authority margin or residual-capability figure to establish how much authority is lost, and whether/how a roll authority reduction is annunciated is not stated (degraded-law annunciation set is [TBD] in AEO-HF-0001 §B.7.1). Without the reduction magnitude the effect that drives the class is unstated.

items.fcDesc: Complete loss of yaw control
items.effAc: No directional control about the yaw axis by any means; a large reduction in functional capabilities that prevents continued safe flight and landing, normally with hull loss, most critically at the engine-out-at-V1 sizing case.
items.effCrew: Crew cannot maintain the intended flight path; hull loss is credited as not recoverable by crew action.
items.effPax: Occupants (flight crew only; hold unoccupied in flight) subject to multiple fatalities with loss of the aircraft.
items.severityRationale: Effects support Catastrophic — "A failure condition that would result in multiple fatalities, usually with the loss of the airplane", AC 25.1309-1B §3.1.5; loss of directional control prevents continued safe flight and landing.

items.severityRationale: Cannot classify: the SDD gives split upper/lower segments each on its own hydraulic supply, but states no residual directional-control margin with one segment lost and no engine-out (V1 sizing case) capability on a single segment. Without the reduction in safety margins the effect produces, the aircraft/crew effect levels cannot be grounded. Needs the flight-control sizing / rudder authority substantiation.

items.effAc: Yaw response differs from that commanded, giving a large reduction in safety margins about the directional axis with the crew aware and acting to counter it.
items.effCrew: Physical distress or excessive workload countering the erroneous response, such that the flightcrew cannot be relied upon to perform their tasks accurately or completely.
items.effPax: Flight crew only aboard; potential serious injury to a small number of persons short of hull loss where the crew arrests the excursion.

items.effAc: Yaw excursion with no crew command, giving a large reduction in safety margins that the crew must counter, most critically during takeoff and approach.
items.effCrew: Physical distress or excessive workload arresting the uncommanded excursion, such that the flightcrew cannot be relied upon to perform their tasks accurately or completely.
items.effPax: Flight crew only aboard; potential serious injury to a small number of persons short of hull loss where the crew arrests the excursion.
items.severityRationale: Effects support Hazardous — "a large reduction in safety margins or functional capabilities", AC 25.1309-1B §3.1.4; carried from the existing SFHA classification for this condition and consistent with the stated effects.

items.effAc: Yaw control authority reduced with the crew unaware; the crew continue their duties normally and take no action, so the reduced margin is not discovered until authority is demanded (e.g. an engine-out or crosswind case).
items.severityRationale: Cannot classify: this is the crew-unaware variant, and the SDD does not state the residual directional margin at the point authority is first demanded, nor whether the reduction defeats the engine-out (V1) sizing case, nor the annunciation coverage of segment/authority loss. Without the reduction in margin the latent state produces, the effect levels cannot be grounded. Per AC 25.1309-1B §5.4.2 loss of annunciation is itself at least Major unless shown otherwise; needs the FCS jam/segment-loss discretes and authority substantiation.

items.effAc: High-lift unavailable; approach and landing flown clean or at the achieved configuration, producing a significant reduction in functional capabilities — higher approach speed and increased landing distance against a 1,800 m requirement with ~1,080 m predicted rollout.
items.effCrew: Significant increase in flightcrew workload to fly a non-normal high-lift configuration approach and re-brief landing performance.
items.effPax: Hold unoccupied in flight; no occupant effect beyond the crew.
items.severityRationale: Effects support "significant reduction in safety margins or functional capabilities", AC 25.1309-1B §3.1.3 — landing performance penalty assessed against the 1,800 m / 1,080 m margin.

items.effPax: Hold unoccupied in flight; no occupant effect beyond the crew.
items.severityRationale: Effects support "large reduction in safety margins or functional capabilities", AC 25.1309-1B §3.1.4 — asymmetric high-lift at low speed with a residual rolling moment.

items.fcDesc: Complete loss of payload restraint — annunciated
items.effAc: The single 72.6 t blade occupying the full 108 m hold is no longer restrained; the payload is one item with no averaging across a distributed load, so a restraint or centre-of-gravity problem is a whole-aircraft problem from the first moment it exists. Payload shift moves the centre of gravity outside the certified envelope and imposes uncommanded loads on the airframe, precluding continued safe flight and resulting in loss of the aircraft.
items.effCrew: Fatalities or incapacitation — the crew are aboard and hull loss is credited as not recoverable by crew action; there is no in-flight adjustment of restraint, the crew has indication only, cannot re-tension and cannot enter the hold in flight.
items.effPax: Multiple fatalities — hull loss with flight crew aboard.
items.severityRationale: Loss of restraint of a single 72.6 t item moving CG outside the certified envelope with no in-flight recovery: "multiple fatalities, usually with the loss of the airplane" (AC 25.1309-1B §3.1.5). The payload is one item — "a restraint or centre-of-gravity problem is a whole-aircraft problem from the first moment it exists" — and the crew has indication only with no means to re-secure it in flight.

Load paths are sized such that the loss of any one strap is carried by its neighbours, but adjacency (not count) is the escalation the design cares about; the residual capability of the restraint set with two adjacent stations lost, and the manoeuvre and turbulence load limit within which the payload stays restrained, are not defined in the provided material.
items.effCrew: Restraint condition annunciated requiring immediate attention; the crew action is a flight-path limitation (minimise manoeuvre load, avoid turbulence, descend/divert, land as soon as possible) because there is nothing the crew can do to the restraint itself in flight — a significant increase in workload with indication only.
items.effPax: None — hold unoccupied in flight; flight crew only.
items.severityRationale: Cannot commit a class: the residual restraint capability with two adjacent stations lost, and the actual manoeuvre/turbulence load limit within which the single 72.6 t item stays restrained, are undefined — HF doc §B.10.2 calls the manoeuvre limitation "the single most important [TBD] in Appendix B" and attaches no procedure to a condition annunciated as "requiring immediate attention". If a wider load envelope breach could progress to CG/structural loss (SF-010-TL), this could be Hazardous or worse; if load paths bound it, it may be lower. Severity left empty pending the restraint load-path analysis and the manoeuvre limit.

items.fcDesc: Complete loss of restraint status monitoring

CONFIRM: the un-annunciated underlying effect is the SF-010 restraint loss, which un-detected is Catastrophic; per §5.4.2 the combination of the restraint loss with loss of its annunciation must meet the objective of the un-annunciated effect, which may drive this above Major — engineer to disposition.

items.effAc: Loss of one or more of the standby attitude/airspeed/altitude parameters while the primary display units and ADIRUs remain available. The primary flight information is unaffected; a subset of the backup layer is degraded. Slight reduction in functional capabilities.
items.effCrew: Slight increase in flightcrew workload; crew continues on the primary displays, notes the degraded standby parameter(s) and treats it as a dispatch/continuation item.
items.effPax: No effect; hold unoccupied in flight, flight crew only.
items.severityRationale: Partial degradation of a backup source with the primary displays fully available is at most a slight reduction. Minor — "a slight reduction in safety margins or functional capabilities", AC 25.1309-1B §3.1.2.

source.quote: Standby attitude, airspeed and altitude are provided by an independent integrated standby instrument

items.fcDesc: Erroneous standby flight information — detected (standby indicates incorrectly, crew aware)
items.effAc: The standby instrument presents incorrect attitude, airspeed or altitude. The crew detects the error by comparison against the primary flight displays (which share no supply, sensor or processing with the standby) and disregards the standby. The primary flight information remains the trusted source; slight reduction in functional capabilities from loss of a usable cross-check.
items.effCrew: Slight increase in flightcrew workload to identify and reject the erroneous standby source and continue on the primary displays.
items.effPax: No effect; hold unoccupied in flight, flight crew only.
items.severityRationale: With the standby dissimilar from and cross-checkable against the primary displays, a detected standby error is rejected and the primary source is retained. Minor — "a slight reduction in safety margins or functional capabilities", AC 25.1309-1B §3.1.2.

source.quote: shares no supply, no sensor and no processing with the primary displays

items.fcDesc: Undetected erroneous standby flight information (standby presents plausible but incorrect data, crew unaware)
items.effAc: The standby presents plausible but incorrect attitude/airspeed/altitude and the crew do not detect it. Its safety consequence depends on whether the standby is being relied upon at the time (i.e. concurrent with primary-display loss or degradation) and on the crew cross-check credited against the dissimilar primary source; the SDD establishes the standby's independence but not the crew detection/response model needed to bound the effect.
items.effPax: No effect; hold unoccupied in flight, flight crew only.
items.severityRationale: Cannot ground the aircraft/crew effect: the outcome turns on the crew cross-check against the primary displays and on whether the standby is being relied upon, and AEO-HF-0001 explicitly does not assign crew tasks, detection or recovery ('what the crew can get wrong, how it would be detected, or how it would be recovered' — §11). Left empty pending the human-factors detection model rather than assumed.

items.fcDesc: Complete loss of engine and APU fire detection and extinguishing
items.effAc: Simultaneous loss of both the means of detecting an engine/APU fire and the means of extinguishing it. An engine or APU fire would then be neither annunciated to the crew nor extinguishable, in a fire zone containing flammable fluid and a high-energy source (Zone 610–640, 800). An undetected, unsuppressed nacelle/APU fire can propagate to adjacent structure and systems and threaten continued safe flight and landing.
items.effPax: No effect from the loss itself; hold unoccupied in flight, flight crew only.
items.severityRationale: The SDD establishes dual-loop detection and two bottles per engine pair, but does not characterise the outcome of a fire that is both undetected and unextinguished (propagation rate, time to structural/systems effect, remaining means). Cannot ground the aircraft effect to a class without that fire-progression/uncontained-fire assessment (cf. §25.851–869 fire protection). Left empty pending that analysis rather than assumed.

source.quote: dual-loop continuous fire detection, with the two loops routed separately

items.fcDesc: Partial loss of fire detection and extinguishing
items.effAc: Fire detection or extinguishing capability is reduced in one or more engine/APU zones; the amount of coverage remaining after this partial loss, and whether an engine fire could go undetected or unextinguished, is not resolvable from the SDD, which states dual-loop AND detection and two cross-plumbed bottles per pair but does not characterise the partial-loss residual.
items.severityRationale: Cannot classify: the SDD describes the full detection/extinguishing architecture but not which capability remains after a partial loss, so no aircraft effect (undetected fire vs still-covered) can be fixed; the levels and severity are left empty pending definition of the partial-loss residual coverage.

source.quote: AND logic between them for warning, degrading to single-loop logic on loss of one loop

items.fcDesc: Erroneous fire warning with no fire (spurious engine/APU fire indication)
items.effAc: A spurious engine or APU fire warning presents with no actual fire; if the crew action it (thrust lever, fuel shut-off, fire handle) an engine is shut down unnecessarily, giving a slight reduction in functional capabilities from the loss of that thrust and its generator/hydraulic/bleed contribution, recoverable on the remaining three engines.
items.effCrew: Crew see the fire warning and read the associated procedure; a significant increase in flightcrew workload arises from diagnosing a fire that is not there and, if actioned, managing an unnecessary shutdown, well within crew capability given the consolidated alert list and associated procedure.
items.effPax: No occupants in the hold; flight crew only, no injury.
items.severityRationale: Major - "significant increase in flightcrew workload", AC 25.1309-1B §3.1.3. The spurious warning and any resulting unnecessary engine shutdown raise workload significantly but remain within crew capability; the aircraft continues on the remaining engines.

source.quote: a single prioritised crew alert list with associated procedures

items.fcDesc: Partial loss of fire detection and extinguishing — single-loop
items.effAc: Loss of one detection loop degrades the AND logic to single-loop logic and is annunciated as a fault; detection remains available on the surviving loop with reduced fault tolerance, and extinguishing is unaffected. The remaining margin against undetected fire on a single loop is not quantified in the SDD.
items.effCrew: The single-loop degradation is annunciated as a fault; the crew note it and manage it as a dispatch/monitoring matter, a slight increase in workload within their capability.
items.effPax: No occupants in the hold; flight crew only, no injury.
items.severityRationale: Minor - "a slight reduction in safety margins or functional capabilities", AC 25.1309-1B §3.1.2. Detection remains on the surviving loop and is annunciated as a fault; only the redundancy of the detection logic is lost, a slight reduction in margin.

items.fcDesc: Inadvertent extinguishing agent discharge
items.effAc: Extinguishing agent discharges into an engine/APU nacelle with no fire present; the affected pair's two cross-plumbed bottles are then partially or wholly expended, so extinguishing capability for a subsequent real fire in that pair is reduced or lost. Whether the discharge itself imposes an immediate operational limitation, and the residual extinguishing capability, are not characterised in the SDD.
items.severityRationale: Cannot classify: the SDD gives two cross-plumbed bottles per engine pair but does not state the effect of an inadvertent discharge (immediate engine/aircraft consequence, or only the loss of extinguishing reserve for a later fire), so no single aircraft effect can be fixed; levels and severity left empty pending that consequence definition.

source.quote: Two extinguisher bottles per engine pair, cross-plumbed so that either bottle can discharge into either nacelle of the pair

items.fcDesc: Undetected loss of fire detection
items.effAc: Fire detection is lost in one or more engine/APU zones without annunciation, so a fire in an affected zone would not be warned to the crew; the crew, unaware, take no fire action and an engine/APU fire could develop unchecked. The design annunciates a single-loop degradation as a fault, so the failure mode by which detection is lost with NO annunciation is not established in the SDD, and the extent of coverage lost is not characterised.
items.effCrew: Crew continue normal duties and take no action, as the loss is by definition undetected; there is no fire warning to prompt them.
items.effPax: No occupants in the hold; flight crew only.
items.severityRationale: Cannot classify: an undetected fire in an engine/APU zone could be severe, but the SDD states loss of a loop is annunciated as a fault, so the failure path producing an UNANNUNCIATED total detection loss and the coverage it removes are not grounded; per AC 25.1309-1B §5.4.2 loss of annunciation is itself a failure condition, but the effect cannot be fixed without the undetected-loss mechanism. Levels and severity left empty pending that mechanism.
